steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Multi-robot tasks often need aerial robots to fly close to each other. This happens in collaborative mapping and exploration missions, where the robots may have to navigate constricted areas, or when the task is in a more limited workspace from the start (ex. indoors). In some cases, such as aerial docking and payload transport, it is actually intended to approach another multirotor closely. In all of these cases the aerodynamic interference from the other vehicles is an additional risk and constraint for the motion planners.

It is possible to extract computational fluid models for multirotors that capture the aerodynamic interactions over the entire state-space of the problem, but such high-fidelity models are often too expensive and restrictive (in computational time and run-time memory), or they are simply not necessary (dynamically transitioning flight modes). For complex and fluid flight missions we need a model of these exogenic forces that is fast and accurate, so that it can facilitate onboard controllers that are robust to these disturbances.

In this work we present a new learning-based approach to estimate the downwash forces that a single multirotor produces. Our equivariant downwash model is different from previous learning-based approaches because it makes assumptions on the geometry that is present in the underlying downwash function. To encode these assumptions in the model, we extract invariant geometric features from the input data, and this decreases the dimensionality of the learning problem. Traditional machine learning algorithms often need large amounts of training data to learn the underlying function accurately, but our algorithm is geometry-aware and sample-efficient.

We train the equivariant downwash model on real-world flight data that was collected by two multirotors using a baseline model-based controller (a linear quadratic regulator, LQR). When we deploy the model online in the controller, it achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on a variety of challenging experiments. To our knowledge the equivariant downwash model is the first learning-based approach that uncovers consistent patterns in the downwash in the lateral plane. We also validate empirically that our model is more sample-efficient than SOTA learning-based approaches.

## I-A Related Work
- Multi-UAS flights
  - growing interest in tight formations in aerial swarms (cite), but few works deploy teams in close proximity
  - downwash deviations trivially minimized by hard inter-agent separation constraints for simplified planners (cite)
  - limits swarm density, excludes navigable airspace; may fail mission due to chaotic, directional single-/multi-agent aerodynamic interactions (cite)

- Learned dynamics

  - discrete-time (residual) dynamics: GPs (cite), RNNs (cite)
  - continuous-time: neural-ODEs + model predictive controllers (cite)
  - extending to inter-vehicle interaction non-trivial: we represent geometric symmetries; modeling their evolution adds sensing + computational complexity
  - SOTA for learning-based downwash prediction: one of the ground-effect works (cite)

- Geometric deep learning

  - represented as invariance/equivariance assumptions on the learned function (cite); discussed in Section III
  - priors ~ "parameter sharing" -> better sample efficiency in various applications (cite)

- Equivariance in robotics

  - equivariant deep- Q learning, soft actor-critic (cite): grasping, picking up/pushing blocks with couple of hours of data (cite)
  - entirely on physical robots (on-robot learning)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Multi-robot tasks often need aerial robots to fly close to each other. This happens in collaborative mapping and exploration missions, where the robots may have to navigate constricted areas, or when the task is in a more limited workspace from the start (ex. indoors). In some cases, such as aerial docking and payload transport, it is actually intended to approach another multirotor closely. In all of these cases the aerodynamic interference from the other vehicles is an additional risk and constraint for the motion planners.

It is possible to extract computational fluid models for multirotors that capture the aerodynamic interactions over the entire state-space of the problem, but such high-fidelity models are often too expensive and restrictive (in computational time and run-time memory), or they are simply not necessary (dynamically transitioning flight modes). For complex and fluid flight missions we need a model of these exogenic forces that is fast and accurate, so that it can facilitate onboard controllers that are robust to these disturbances.

In this work we present a new learning-based approach to estimate the downwash forces that a single multirotor produces. Our equivariant downwash model is different from previous learning-based approaches because it makes assumptions on the geometry that is present in the underlying downwash function. To encode these assumptions in the model, we extract invariant geometric features from the input data, and this decreases the dimensionality of the learning problem. Traditional machine learning algorithms often need large amounts of training data to learn the underlying function accurately, but our algorithm is geometry-aware and sample-efficient.

We train the equivariant downwash model on real-world flight data that was collected by two multirotors using a baseline model-based controller (a linear quadratic regulator, LQR). When we deploy the model online in the controller, it achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on a variety of challenging experiments. To our knowledge the equivariant downwash model is the first learning-based approach that uncovers consistent patterns in the downwash in the lateral plane. We also validate empirically that our model is more sample-efficient than SOTA learning-based approaches.

## I-A Related Work

Multi-UAS Flights. There is recent and increasing interest in the problem of tight formations in aerial swarms, but there is a dearth of work that tries to deploy teams in close proximity. The forces induced by downwash, and the deviations from planned trajectories that result, can be trivially minimized by enforcing hard separation constraints between agents that are large enough for simplified motion planners. These approaches severely limit the swarm density that can be achieved, because they naïvely exclude navigable airspace, and worse, they may fail their mission objectives because both single- and multi-agent aerodynamic interactions are chaotic and directional.

Recent work has combined nominal dynamics models based on physics with deep neural networks (DNN) to predict and counteract exogenous forces from ground effect or from neighboring multirotors. Modeling the discrete-time (residual) dynamics of a multirotor has also been studied, for instance with Gaussian processes (GPs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). Others learned the continuous-time dynamics directly using neural ordinary differential equations (neural-ODEs) together with model predictive controllers. But it can be non-trivial to extend these works to model the interaction dynamics between vehicles. This is because in this work we are representing the geometric symmetries in the problem, and modeling how they evolve adds sensing and computational complexities. So we consider the model from one of the ground effect works above to be the SOTA for learning-based downwash prediction.

Geometric Deep Learning. Geometric deep learning at its core means imposing inductive biases (called "geometric priors") on the learning algorithm through one's knowledge of the geometry of the problem. We will discuss in Section III that these geometric priors are represented with assumptions of invariance and equivariance on the underlying function that is learned. The point of geometric priors is that intuitively they correspond to "parameter sharing", and so they have been shown to improve sample efficiency in various applications.

In robotics, equivariant reinforcement learning has been used for low-level quadrotor control and for robot manipulation tasks. In particular, recent research developed equivariant deep- Q learning and soft actor-critic algorithms that can learn complex manipulation tasks (ex. grasping, picking up and pushing blocks) with only a couple of hours of training data. These learning algorithms were run entirely on physical robots (i.e. on-robot learning). To our knowledge no previous work has used geometric priors to learn multirotor downwash forces efficiently.

## I-B Contributions

Our work has the following key contributions:

- 1. We propose a model for multirotor downwash that is equivariant and makes assumptions on the geometry of the downwash field. This model is geometry-aware and represents the data in a lower-dimensional space so that the assumed rotational equivariance of our system is satisfied.

- 2. We give real-world experimental results that show the sample efficiency of our equivariant downwash model. With only 5 minutes of flight data we learn the downwash function more accurately than SOTA learning-based approaches do with 15 minutes of data.

- 3. When it is deployed online in an optimal feedback controller, the predictions of our model reduce vertical tracking errors by 56\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} and lateral tracking errors by 36\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}.

Modeling the discrete-time (residual) dynamics of a multirotor has also been studied using, for instance, Gaussian processes (GPs) [18] and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) [19]. Others have directly learned the continuous-time dynamics using neural ordinary differential equations (neural-ODEs) combined with model predictive controllers [20,21]. However, extending these works to model inter-vehicle interaction dynamics can be non-trivial, because in this work we represent the geometric symmetries in the problem, and modeling their evolution adds sensing and computational complexity. We therefore consider the model from [14] the SOTA for learning-based downwash prediction.

Geometric Deep Learning. At its core, geometric deep learning involves imposing inductive biases (called "geometric priors") on the learning algorithm via knowledge of the problem geometry. As discussed in Section III, these geometric priors are represented as assumptions of invariance and equivariance on the underlying function being learned [22,23]. Geometric priors intuitively correspond to "parameter sharing," and have thus been shown to improve sample efficiency across various applications [24,25].

Within robotics, equivariant reinforcement learning has been employed for low-level quadrotor control [26] and robot manipulation tasks [27,28]. In particular, recent research has developed equivariant deep- Q learning and soft actor-critic algorithms [25] capable of learning complex manipulation tasks (ex. grasping, picking up and pushing blocks) from only a couple of hours of training data [27,28]. These algorithms were trained entirely on physical robots (i.e. on-robot learning). To our knowledge, no previous work has utilized geometric priors to efficiently learn multirotor downwash forces.

## I-B Contributions

The key contributions of our work are:

- 1. We propose an equivariant model for multirotor downwash that makes assumptions on the geometry of the downwash field. This geometry-aware model represents data in a lower-dimensional space in order to satisfy the assumed rotational equivariance of our system.

- 2. We provide real-world experimental results showcasing the sample efficiency of our equivariant downwash model. Using only 5 minutes of flight data, we learn the downwash function more accurately than SOTA learning-based approaches do with 15 minutes of data.

- 3. When deployed online within an optimal feedback controller, our model's predictions reduce vertical tracking errors by 56\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} and lateral tracking errors by 36\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}.
